title: File search and retrieval (RAG)
trust_boundary: Before: the model answers from training and the prompt. After: passages retrieved from a document store are placed in the prompt and treated as knowledge. Whoever can add or edit a document can put text in the model's context.
Retrieval runs as some identity. If the index was built with wider access than the asking user has, an answer can cross a permission boundary.
Documents, chunks and embeddings are copied into a store with its own access control, retention and location, often the vendor's.
Answers carry citations, and people trust citations.
context_questions: Which repositories are indexed, and who can write to them?
Whose permissions apply at query time: the asking user's, or the indexer's?
Where does the index live, and who operates it?

threats.title: Planted documents steer answers or carry instructions
threats.description: A document written to be retrieved changes what the model says or does for other users.
questions: Who can add or edit indexed content: all staff, customers, the public?
Is retrieved text marked as data? Can it trigger tool calls?
Is there review or provenance for content entering the index?
vendor_evidence: Any filtering at ingestion or retrieval.

own_tests.how: against your own endpoint with documents you plant in a test index.
a fixed prompt set against the same endpoint.

no_standard_test: Your corpus and your ingestion path.

threats.title: Retrieval returns what the asking user may not see
threats.description: The index was built by an account with wide access, or access rules are not applied at query time, or they are stale.
questions: Are source-system permissions enforced per query, per user?
How quickly does a permission change in the source reach the index?
vendor_evidence: The permission model of the retrieval feature.
no_standard_test: Needs your access rules: a test with two accounts of different rights. No public benchmark.

threats.title: Secrets and personal data become searchable
threats.description: Credentials or personal data sitting in indexed documents can now be asked for in plain language.
questions: Was the corpus checked for secrets and regulated data before indexing?
Can repositories or file types be excluded?
no_standard_test: A scan of your own corpus. Outside this repo.

threats.title: Leakage between tenants or projects in a shared index
threats.description: One customer's or project's passages are retrieved for another.
questions: Is the index per tenant, per project, or shared with filtering?
What is the vendor's isolation evidence?

threats.title: Private content leaves through the rendered answer
threats.description: Retrieved text is placed in a link or image address that the user's client fetches, sending it to an attacker.
questions: Does the client render links and remote images from model output?
Is there an allowlist of domains?

own_tests.how: against your endpoint, watching for outbound requests that carry a canary.

no_standard_test: Depends on your client. No public benchmark for a given product.

threats.title: Wrong answers with trustworthy-looking citations
threats.description: Conflicting, promotional or fabricated passages are presented with citations that make them look checked.
questions: Do users act on answers without opening the sources?
Does the product show which passage supports which claim?
vendor_evidence: Evaluations of answer faithfulness and citation accuracy.

threats.title: The store itself: location, retention, deletion
threats.description: Copies of documents and embeddings sit somewhere new, are kept after the source is deleted, or are used for other purposes.
questions: Where are chunks and embeddings stored, for how long, and are they used for training?
Does deleting a source document remove its chunks and embeddings?
vendor_evidence: Data-handling terms that name the retrieval store.
